claims.feature: incidental figure given a full death
claims.claim: Rettino cites the Kanlin messenger killed with Spring Rain's letter, an 'incidental figure' living the drama of his own life and death, as Kay's device for showing history's lost documents.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: living through the drama and passion of his own life

claims.claim: Rettino argues Kay's endings grant refuge to a few characters rather than reversing historical catastrophe: a happy ending weighted with sorrow.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: a happy ending, though one weighted with sorrow

claims.claim: Rettino notes Jehane sees 'a good man raise his sword and... a good man fall' with deliberate ambiguity, resolved only in the epilogue.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: With deliberate ambiguity on Kay’s part

claims.claim: Rettino reads Tai's recognition scene as a false assumption about his role in shaping history, with Sima Zian calling such knowledge arrogance.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: a false assumption about his role in shaping history

claims.claim: Rettino cites the narrator's essayistic passage that humans demand order and pattern in the flux of history, exposing Kay's own patterning.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: questions the integrity of historical narratives

claims.claim: Rettino notes Under Heaven closes on two unnamed men burying the dead until they die and the spirits fall silent.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: not even the dead can grieve forever

claims.claim: Rettino reads Ammar's closing poem as setting an elegiac tone, with children's laughter audible through the window.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: The poem sets an elegiac tone

claims.claim: Rettino reads Baerd carrying memory 'like a cart yoked to his shoulders' and Alessan's blade-in-the-soul oath as memory chosen as bondage rather than escape.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: like a cart yoked to his shoulders

claims.claim: Rettino terms Kay's settings 'mirror worlds' that distort a historical original so its story can be projected onto other contexts.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: The Palm is a “mirror world” of Italy

claims.claim: Rettino, via Mendlesohn, finds it troubling that Tigana relies on the incontestable club-story authority of guides (Baerd, Alessan) in a novel about how power controls history.
claims.source: Matthew Rettino, 'Fantasies of History: Guy Gavriel Kay's Synthesis of the Historical Fantasy Novel' (Honours thesis, McGill University, 2012)
claims.quote: it is somewhat troubling that Kay should choose

claims.claim: Cobb argues Kay's enrichment of the reader is primarily emotional rather than rational, helping readers bear the burden of history rather than master it.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings

claims.claim: Cobb reads the Tigana oath as memory that is both a wound and a rod of support.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings
claims.quote: This memory is both a wound and a rod of support

claims.claim: Cobb notes it is perfectly possible to read Tigana without knowing it recasts Renaissance Italy, so its revision uncomfortably resembles the tyrant's spell.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings
claims.quote: perfectly possible to read the novel without any awareness

claims.claim: Cobb observes that the Sarantine Mosaic's minimal adaptation of place-names and extensive acknowledgements force the reader to recognise actual history.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings

claims.claim: Cobb reads Crispin's mosaic as an analogy for Kay's own project of re-creating history in art.
claims.source: Christopher Cobb, 'Guy Gavriel Kay and the Psychology of History', Foundation (Summer 2005), reprinted on Bright Weavings
claims.quote: makes an analogy between his own artistic project and Crispin’s

verdicts.trueWording: Kanlin Warrior with Spring Rain's letter, ambushed and killed
verdicts.note: Raw page (brightweavings, Rettino thesis) has verbatim: 'this "incidental figure" who "is living through the drama and passion of his own life and death," is that he is ambushed and killed, the letter "tumbling in dust and wind, and disappearing" (702-703).' The lost-documents limb is the framing sentence: 'Authority is also questioned in the context of the survival of historical documents; since not all documents survive...' and 'Such lost documentation exposes the fault in a Scholastic system of knowledge.'

verdicts.trueWording: Eucatastrophe more local; does not recover an entire nation
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: 'providing a happy ending, though one weighted with sorrow. Eucatastrophe occurs, but it is more local and does not entail the recovery of an entire nation.' The generalising limb ('Kay's endings', refuge not reversal) is separately supported on the same page: 'By granting his characters "refuge" from massacres, sieges, and civil war... he ends his stories on a satisfying note without having to reverse the downward cycle of the decay of empires... a eucatastrophe in this sense might change a few individuals.'

verdicts.trueWording: Only in the epilogue does it become clear Ammar won
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'With deliberate ambiguity on Kay's part, Jehane watches the battle and sees "a good man raise his sword and … a good man fall" (620). Only in the epilogue does it become clear that Ammar is the victor.' Every limb (Jehane, the inner quotation, deliberate ambiguity, epilogue resolution) is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Recognition is a false assumption; Zian calls such knowing arrogance
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'a moment in which the protagonist makes a false assumption about his role in shaping history.' The Zian limb: 'Sima Zian, a poet who is Tai's friend, says that "the idea we can know what must be done, and do it properly" is "arrogance" (372).'

verdicts.trueWording: Narrator's reflections expose a gap between flux and Kay's patterning
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Kay's narrator questions the integrity of historical narratives...'. The cited passage is block-quoted on the page: 'we seek-even demand-order and pattern in our lives, in the flow and flux of history and our own times' (330-331). The self-exposure limb: 'The narrator's reflections expose a gap between how the narrator conceives of history as flux and how Kay uses a story with a patterned narrative,' plus 'he alludes obliquely to his own role in shaping his narrative.'

verdicts.trueWording: Final image: two unnamed men burying dead until both die
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'The final image of the novel is that of two unnamed men (most likely Shen Tai and Sima Zian) who continue to bury the dead, until both men die, one after the other. Eventually "because not even the dead can grieve forever, forgotten, there came a moonlit night when there was no lost spirit crying in Kuala Nor" (710).'

verdicts.trueWording: Poem sets elegiac tone; children's laughter through an open window
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'The poem sets an elegiac tone to the end of the novel.' Immediately followed by 'Ammar speaks his poem while he hears his "children's laughter … through an open window" (634).' The poem is Ammar's epilogue lament ('Where are Tudesca, Elvira, Aljais...').

verdicts.trueWording: Alessan subjects himself to bondage instead of escaping it
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Baerd carrying his own memory of his country "like a cart yoked to his shoulders"...'. The oath limb is on the same page: 'Somewhat paradoxically, Alessan utters his oath, "Tigana, let my memory of you be like a blade in my soul," to subject himself to bondage, instead of seeking to escape it (158),' and the section frames memory as a form of bondage.

verdicts.trueWording: A distorted mirror reflecting onto a host of other contexts
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'The Palm is a "mirror world" of Italy, though it is a distorted mirror, capable of reflecting an image removed from its specifics onto a host of other contexts: colonial dominance over Africa, the Caribbean, native North America, and even Eastern Europe under the Communist Bloc.' The plural 'mirror worlds' for Kay's settings also appears: 'Kay's "mirror worlds," while they may separate narratives from their historical contexts and distort them...'

verdicts.trueWording: Portal-quest relies on incontestable authority of a narrative persona
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'In a novel that is precisely about how power influences how history is understood, it is somewhat troubling that Kay should choose to compose a portal-quest fantasy, which relies on the incontestable authority of a narrative persona.' Club-story limb supported: 'Club-story narrators, Alessan and Baerd could have multiple motives for distorting the truth'; guide limb: 'the protagonist cannot interpret events without a guide'; Mendlesohn is the cited authority throughout (Mendlesohn 5-7, 17).

verdicts.trueWording: Enrichment emotional, helping readers deal with history's burden
verdicts.note: Raw page (brightweavings /hspsychologyhistory/) verbatim: 'Kay's work offers an enrichment for its readers that is primarily emotional rather than rational. It helps them deal with the burden of history in their memories...'. The 'rather than master it' limb is the explicit contrast with alternate history's 'rational mastery of the historical process,' which Kay's fiction 'rejects.'

verdicts.trueWording: Oath quoted, then: memory both a wound and support
verdicts.note: Verbatim, and directly after the Tigana oath: 'the oath that gives the first part of the book its title: "Tigana, let my memory of you be like a blade in my soul." This memory is both a wound and a rod of support.'

verdicts.trueWording: Uncomfortable resemblance to the tyrant's spell
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'it is perfectly possible to read the novel without any awareness that it is a re-casting of Renaissance Italy.' Next sentences: 'The novel's failure to acknowledge Tigana's relationship to actual history renders its revision of that history problematic. If a reader enjoys Tigana but never learns the history of Italy, then Kay's revision of that history bears an uncomfortable resemblance to the tyrant's spell.'

verdicts.trueWording: Require the reader to recognize the actual history
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Kay's minimal adaptation of place-names (Sarantium) and his extensive acknowledgements section require the reader to recognize the actual history that the novels take up, to face its losses.' The sentence is explicitly about the Sarantine Mosaic ('The Sarantine Mosaic, then, makes clear the value of its imaginative restoration of Byzantium').

verdicts.trueWording: Kay's 'mosaic' analogises his project to Crispin's
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Kay's use of "mosaic" in his novel makes an analogy between his own artistic project and Crispin's.' Surrounding text supports the re-creating-history limb: 'Their artistic re-creations of history for their world reflect upon Kay's project of creating such histories for our own,' and 'The value of re-creating history in art appears most clearly in the life of the mosaicist Caius Crispus.'
